doc.title: Sonny Igoe interviewed by Monk Rowe, Emerson, New Jersey, July 31, 2003

title: Setting up for the Gene Krupa drum contest
summary: At 16 Igoe enters Krupa's amateur drum contest at the Meadowbrook with a junky kit, and recalls Joe Mooney and his mother's Hammond organ.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: Uh huh. Didn’t you win a Gene Krupa contest?

Yes I did. That’s what I’m sort of leading up to. I was very — well I always say I was lucky because I was only 16, and Gene had — the publicity got out — excuse me is this legal? The publicity came out that Gene was going to have a drum contest for amateur drummers, kids. And so he called up and talked to the people at the Meadowbrook or whoever, and I called up — my mother called up I guess — no it was my grandmother called up. Because she lived in East Orange and she heard about, she called up and told them about me. So they took our number and they called us and we went that afternoon. And there were about 40 drummers. And we were set up on the dance floor at the Meadowbrook. And Gene didn’t know how to handle it quite, because it’s the first time he had did that and he didn’t expect that many guys to begin with. And the majority of the fellas came with these very glamorous sets just like Gene’s. I had a junky, terrible, as a matter of fact half of it was in this picture here where you really can’t see much but look how old fashioned that is. That would really hold back, with the temple block and the tom toms that you tune, that was called Chinese tom toms. And I was about that age.
Did you have a hi hat?
Yes, right over here. See this great big thing here?
That’s what they called a hi hat in those days. Those cymbals were awful. They were just terrible. But anyway that’s what my set looked like.
I’m so glad — look at — you have the chair.
Yes and I put a pillow so I could sit high enough.

I didn’t have any stool or something. Anyway but that’s what my set was the pits. Everybody else had great drums. So anyway I had had the good fortune to have met a fellow named Joe Mooney who was a marvelous musician from Paterson. He was blind. He played accordion like you never heard. It sounded like a brass section when he played the accordion. It was just great. He was a marvelous arranger. And my mother had a Hammond organ. My mother was a fine pianist. She had a Hammond organ when they first came out. And they asked her if it would be all right if they used her organ and our house for a demonstration, for appointments. And I don’t know what kind of — if she got paid for that or anything like that or if they gave her the organ probably or something like that. Anyway Joe Mooney heard about it and came up and he played the organ and you couldn’t get my mother away from him, because when he played the organ he was unbelievable. So he brought some guys up and they let me jam with them. And they really taught me how to play on those jam sessions. It was great.
